claim: Mice trained to intravenously self-administer heroin under a fixed-ratio one schedule for 12 daily sessions of 6 hr maximum quickly learned to discriminate between an active and an inactive lever.
source: Mice were trained to intravenously self-administer heroin under a fixed-ratio one schedule (Figure 1a, see Methods) for 12 daily sessions of 6 hr maximum (Figure 1b). The dose was decreased from 50 to 25 µg/kg/infusion after six days, which led to higher acquisition rates (Figure 1c). The animals quickly learned to discriminate between an active and an inactive lever (after 6 days of training: 144.9 ± 26.0 active lever presses versus 8.3 ± 2.5 inactive ones; after 12 days: 283.4 ± 28 versus 20.9 ± 9.3. Figure 1d–f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential lever pressing behavior (144.9 ± 26.0 active vs 8.3 ± 2.5 inactive after 6 days) and referenced to Figure 1d-f showing behavioral measurements.

claim: After 30 days of withdrawal, mice significantly differentiated between active and inactive lever in the absence of heroin injections.
source: After 30d of withdrawal, mice were brought back into the apparatus in the absence of heroin injections and significantly differentiated between active and inactive lever (Figure 1h and i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from withdrawal testing and referenced to Figure 1h and i showing lever discrimination behavior.

claim: Heroin is highly reinforcing and induces seeking behavior, which is a widely used model for relapse.
source: Taken together this experiment shows that heroin was highly reinforcing and induced seeking behavior, a widely used model for relapse (García Pardo et al., 2017; Shaham et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the self-administration and withdrawal experiments, and by citations to García Pardo et al., 2017 and Shaham et al., 2003 establishing this as a model for relapse.

claim: dLight1 enables optical readout of changes in DA concentration by coupling the agonist binding-induced conformational changes in human DA receptors to changes in the fluorescence intensity of circularly permuted GFP derived from GCaMP6.
source: dLight1 enables optical readout of changes in DA concentration by coupling the agonist binding-induced conformational changes in human DA receptors to changes in the fluorescence intensity of circularly permuted (cp) GFP derived from GCaMP6 (Patriarchi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patriarchi et al., 2018 describing the dLight1 sensor mechanism.

claim: Brief (5 ms) delivery of 593 nm laser light pulses into the VTA resulted in an increase of fluorescence in the NAc that co-varied with frequency of stimulation.
source: Brief (5 ms) delivery of 593 nm laser light pulses into the VTA resulted in an increase of fluorescence in the NAc that co-varied with frequency of stimulation (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation experiments and referenced to Figure 2d showing frequency-dependent fluorescence changes.

claim: Within less than a minute after intraperitoneal heroin administration, a fluorescence transient was observed that peaked after three minutes.
source: Within less than a minute after the intraperitoneal heroin administration, we observed the onset of a fluorescence transient that peaked after three minutes (Figure 2e–f, saline: −0.008 ± 0.007, dF/F heroin: 0.133 ± 0.03 dF/F, p=0.0062, t(6) = 4.117, Paired Student's T-Test, n = 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing time course and magnitude of fluorescence changes with statistical analysis (p=0.0062, n=7) and referenced to Figure 2e-f.

claim: The effect size of heroin on dLight fluorescence was similar to that of cocaine.
source: Importantly, the effect size was similar to that of cocaine, but was not seen following administration of the selective-serotonin reuptake inhibitor citalopram nor the norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor reboxetine (Figure 2g saline: −0.01 ± 0.005 dF/F, citalopram: −0.008 ± 0.008 dF/F, cocaine: 0.165 ± 0.025 dF/F, reboxetine −0.009 ± 0.006 dF/F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing fluorescence changes across different drugs (heroin: 0.133 ± 0.03 dF/F vs cocaine: 0.165 ± 0.025 dF/F) and referenced to Figure 2g.

claim: dLight fluorescence specifically captures dopamine transients.
source: These experiments demonstrate that dLight fluorescence specifically captures dopamine transients, and a first injection of heroin increases DA concentration in the NAc within minutes.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing selective response to dopamine-modulating drugs (heroin, cocaine) but not to serotonin or norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors.

claim: A first injection of heroin increases DA concentration in the NAc within minutes.
source: These experiments demonstrate that dLight fluorescence specifically captures dopamine transients, and a first injection of heroin increases DA concentration in the NAc within minutes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing fluorescence increase within minutes of heroin administration (peaked after three minutes).

claim: Repeated infusions of heroin through the jugular vein every 2 min increased the calcium signal in VTA-DA neurons within minutes and a plateau is observed after the third infusion.
source: Repeated infusions of heroin through the jugular vein, every 2 min, increased the calcium signal in VTA-DA neurons within minutes and a plateau is observed after the third infusion (Figure 2i–j, dF/F saline compared to baseline: −0.0063 ± 0.016, dF/F heroin compared to baseline: 0.22 ± 0.085, n = 11, p=0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GCaMP6m recordings showing calcium signal changes with statistical analysis (p=0.001, n=11) and referenced to Figure 2i-j.

claim: The kinetic of VTA DA neuron activity is similar to the DA surge observed in the NAc suggesting a tight correlation between VTA DA neurons activity and DA release.
source: Interestingly, even though the methods are inherently technically different, the kinetic of this activity is similar to the DA surge we observed in the NAc suggesting a tight correlation between VTA DA neurons activity and DA release.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of temporal patterns between VTA DA neuron calcium signals and NAc dopamine fluorescence measurements.

claim: The first exposure to heroin in naive animals increases VTA DA neuron activity and increases DA release in the NAc.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that the first exposure to heroin in naive animals increases VTA DA neuron activity and increases DA release in the NAc.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both GCaMP6m recordings in VTA and dLight recordings in NAc showing increased activity and DA release.

claim: 27.8% of TH+ neurons were cFos+ after heroin self-administration in the medial part of the VTA, whereas 1.5% of TH+ were cFos+ after saline self-administration.
source: Cells positive for cFos that were also TH-immunoreactive were found most prominently in the medial part of the VTA. In this area of the VTA, 27.8% of TH+ were cFos+ after heroin SA, whereas 1.5% of TH+ were cFos+ after saline SA (Figure 3b–e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry showing differential cFos expression (27.8% vs 1.5%) and referenced to Figure 3b-e.

claim: DA neurons located in the medial part of the VTA preferentially project to the NAc core and medial Shell as well as in the medial prefrontal cortex, whereas DA neurons located in more lateral portions of the VTA project to the lateral Shell.
source: DA neurons located in the medial part of the VTA preferentially project to the NAc core and medial Shell as well as in the medial prefrontal cortex, whereas DA neurons located in more lateral portions of the VTA project to the lateral Shell (Lammel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lammel et al., 2008 describing VTA-NAc projection topography.

claim: CTB-555 seeded in the medial NAc retrogradely migrated to the medial VTA, whereas CTB-455 injected into the lateral Shell was mostly found in the lateral VTA, with very little co-localization of the two tracers (1.5%).
source: CTB-555 seeded in the medial NAc retrogradly migrated to the medial VTA, whereas CTB-455 injected into the lateral Shell was mostly found in the lateral VTA, with very little co-localization of the two tracers (1.5%, Figure 3g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing showing spatial segregation (1.5% co-localization) and referenced to Figure 3g.

claim: There are very few collaterals between medial and lateral VTA-NAc projections.
source: This result indicates that there are very few collaterals (Yang et al., 2018), allowing for a quantification of the co-localization of the two CTB markers with cFos after a first heroin self-administration session.
evidence: Inferred from the low co-localization data (1.5%) and supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: 51.0% of medial Shell projecting VTA neurons were cFos positive after heroin self-administration, while this was only the case in 20.5% lateral Shell projecting cells.
source: We found that 51.0% of medial Shell projecting VTA neurons were also cFos positive, while this was only the case in 20.5% lateral Shell projecting cells. (Figure 3h–j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from combined retrograde tracing and cFos immunohistochemistry (51.0% vs 20.5%) and referenced to Figure 3h-j.

claim: Heroin self-administration activates DA neurons in the medial part of the VTA that project preferentially to the medial NAc shell.
source: Taken together, heroin self-administration activates DA neurons in the medial part of the VTA that project preferentially to the medial NAc shell.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cFos mapping and retrograde tracing showing preferential activation of medial VTA neurons projecting to medial NAc shell.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of VTA DA neurons in animals where self-administration was well established significantly decreased the number of active lever presses and ensuing heroin infusions.
source: Silencing VTA DA neurons in animals where self-administration was well established significantly decreased the number of active lever presses and ensuing heroin infusions (Figure 4c–e, 223 ± 60 LP for 111 ± 25 infusions dropped to 23 ± 9 LP for 15 ± 6 infusions after 4 days of treatment condition (DAT-Cre+ versus DAT-Cre-) x CNO (present, absent), two-way repeated measures ANOVA and multiple comparison post-hoc Sidack test, *p<0.05, **p<0.005, ****p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic manipulation showing significant behavioral changes with statistical analysis (p<0.0001) and referenced to Figure 4c-e.

claim: Silencing VTA DA neurons from the first to the fourth session significantly prevented the acquisition of heroin self-administration.
source: Silencing VTA DA neurons from the first to the fourth session significantly prevented the acquisition of heroin SA (Figure 4f–h). After CNO was stopped (from session 5), the mice quickly acquired the task and reached a number of lever presses and infusions similar to the control animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic manipulation during early acquisition showing prevention of learning and referenced to Figure 4f-h.

claim: CNO had no effect on self-administration in DAT-Cre- mice.
source: CNO had no effect on self-administration in DAT-Cre- mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from control animals lacking Cre recombinase, serving as negative control for chemogenetic manipulation.

claim: VTA DA activity is required for the initial reinforcing properties of opioids from the very early stage of drug exposure.
source: All together these results suggest that VTA DA activity is required for the initial reinforcing properties of opioids from the very early stage of drug exposure.
evidence: Inferred from the chemogenetic inhibition experiments showing that blocking VTA DA neurons prevents acquisition and maintenance of heroin self-administration.

claim: Heroin decreased lever-pressing for VTA DA neuron self-stimulation in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: At baseline, the mice pressed up to 291 ± 39 times to obtain 134 ± 1.15 LS in 60 min under a fixed-ratio 1 (FR1, followed by 20 s time out period) schedule (Figure 5d and e). After heroin injection, the performance decreased significantly in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 5i), suppressing lever pressing completely at the highest dose (Figure 5d–i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic self-stimulation experiments showing dose-dependent decrease in lever pressing and referenced to Figure 5d-i.

claim: Heroin increases locomotor activity in open field, even at the highest dose tested.
source: To rule out any sedative effects of heroin at these doses, a separate set of mice were tested over a 30 min free exploration period in an open field (see Methods). We observed that heroin actually increases locomotor activity in open field, even at the highest dose tested (Figure 5j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from open field locomotor testing and referenced to Figure 5j.

claim: Reinforcement induced by optogenetic self-stimulation of VTA DA neurons or heroin self-administration share underlying neural circuits.
source: These experiments indicate that reinforcement induced by optogenetic self-stimulation of VTA DA neurons or heroin SA share underlying neural circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the occlusion experiment showing that heroin blocks optogenetic self-stimulation of VTA DA neurons.

claim: Mice expressing eArchT-3.0 in VTA GABA neurons quickly learned to discriminate the active and inactive lever by significantly increasing the number of active lever press and laser-stimulation triggered during the acquisition sessions.
source: We expressed the light-gated inhibitory proton pump eArchT-3.0 in the VTA of GAD-Cre mice (Figure 6a–b; O'Connor et al., 2015) and gave the mice control over the laser switch. The mice quickly learned to discriminate the active and inactive lever by significantly increasing the number of active lever press and laser-stimulation triggered during the acquisition sessions (293.1 ± 40 LP to obtain 119 ± 15 LS in 180 min).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic self-inhibition experiments showing learned discrimination behavior and referenced to Figure 6a-b and citation to O'Connor et al., 2015.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of heroin just prior to the VTA GABA self-inhibition session significantly decreased the operant behavior in a dose-dependent manner and abolished this behavior at the highest dose.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of heroin just prior to the VTA GABA self-inhibition session significantly decreased the operant behavior in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6d–f) and abolished this behavior at the highest dose (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic self-inhibition with heroin administration showing dose-dependent behavioral suppression and referenced to Figure 6d-f.

claim: The IC50 for heroin occlusion of VTA GABA self-inhibition was very similar to the IC50 calculated based on the occlusion with DA neuron self-stimulation (6.9 vs 6.4 mg/kg).
source: In fact, the IC50 was very similar to the IC50 calculated based on the occlusion with DA neuron self-stimulation (6.9 vs 6.4 mg/kg, Figure 6i and Figure 5i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing IC50 values from two different occlusion experiments and referenced to Figure 6i and Figure 5i.

claim: Reinforcement by optogenetic VTA GABA self-inhibition and reinforcement by heroin share underlying neural circuits.
source: This experiment indicates that reinforcement by optogenetic VTA GABA self-inhibition and reinforcement by heroin share underlying neural circuits and are compatible with a disinhibitory mechanism where heroin targets GABA neurons leading to an increase of DA neurons activity.
evidence: Inferred from the occlusion experiment showing that heroin blocks VTA GABA self-inhibition with similar IC50 to DA neuron self-stimulation occlusion.

claim: Heroin employs a disinhibitory mechanism where heroin targets GABA neurons leading to an increase of DA neurons activity.
source: This experiment indicates that reinforcement by optogenetic VTA GABA self-inhibition and reinforcement by heroin share underlying neural circuits and are compatible with a disinhibitory mechanism where heroin targets GABA neurons leading to an increase of DA neurons activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of VTA GABA self-inhibition occlusion and VTA DA neuron activation experiments.

claim: Heroin activates DA neurons located in the medial part of the VTA, preferentially projecting to the medial shell of the nucleus accumbens.
source: In the present study, we found that heroin increases DA in the NAc through the activation of a subset of VTA DA neurons located in the medial VTA, which preferentially project to the NAc medial shell.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cFos mapping, retrograde tracing, and photometry experiments showing preferential activation of medial VTA neurons projecting to medial NAc shell.

claim: Chemo- and optogenetic manipulations support a disinhibitory motif and establish a link of causality with behavioral reinforcement.
source: Our chemo- and optogenetic manipulations support a disinhibitory motif and establish a link of causality with behavioral reinforcement.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic inhibition of DA neurons and optogenetic self-stimulation/self-inhibition experiments.

claim: The VTA consists of DA (60–65%), GABA (30–35%), glutamate (2%) and neurons that express more than one marker.
source: The VTA consists of DA (60–65%), GABA (30–35%), glutamate (2%) and neurons that express more than one marker (Margolis et al., 2006; Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Roberts and Ribak, 1987; Steffensen et al., 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Margolis et al., 2006; Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Roberts and Ribak, 1987; Steffensen et al., 1998; Yamaguchi et al., 2011) describing VTA cellular composition.

claim: Aversive stimuli potentiate glutamatergic inputs onto DA neurons projecting to the mPFC, while rewarding stimuli potentiate inputs onto medial shell and lateral shell NAc projecting DA neurons.
source: For example, aversive stimuli potentiate glutamatergic inputs onto DA neurons projecting to the mPFC, while rewarding stimuli potentiate inputs onto medial shell and lateral shell NAc projecting DA neurons (Lammel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lammel et al., 2011 describing stimulus-specific synaptic plasticity in VTA DA neuron subpopulations.

claim: The mediolateral topography of accumbens shell neurons is conserved by their dopamine inputs from the VTA, where medial and lateral shell projecting DA neurons segregate along the mediolateral VTA.
source: The mediolateral topography of accumbens shell neurons is conserved by their dopamine inputs from the VTA, where medial and lateral shell projecting DA neurons segregate along the mediolateral VTA (Beier et al., 2015; Lammel et al., 2012; Lammel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Beier et al., 2015; Lammel et al., 2012; Lammel et al., 2008) describing VTA-NAc topographic organization.

claim: Heroin during initial reinforcement preferentially activates neurons of the medial VTA projecting to the medial Shell.
source: We find that heroin during initial reinforcement preferentially activates neurons of the medial VTA projecting to the medial Shell, but cannot exclude the contribution from other projections.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cFos mapping and retrograde tracing showing preferential activation (51.0% vs 20.5% for medial vs lateral projections).

claim: Most of the afferents to midbrain DA neurons are GABAergic.
source: Most of the afferents to midbrain DA neurons are GABAergic.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about VTA circuitry and afferent connectivity.

claim: Back projecting accumbal medium-spiny neurons, while targeting both DA and GABA neurons, form particularly strong synaptic connections to the latter.
source: Back projecting accumbal medium-spiny neurons, while targeting both DA and GABA neurons (Beier et al., 2015; Henny et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018), form particularly strong synaptic connections to the latter (Bocklisch et al., 2013), which then control the activity of DA neurons (Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies describing NAc-VTA connectivity (Beier et al., 2015; Henny et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018; Bocklisch et al., 2013; Johnson and North, 1992).

claim: This disinhibitory motif is particularly strong for neurons of the lateral VTA.
source: This disinhibitory motif is particularly strong for neurons of the lateral VTA (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018 describing regional differences in disinhibitory circuitry.

claim: Removal of tonic inhibition from VTA DA neurons by interneurons and accumbal projections can cause increases in DA neuron activity and NAc DA release.
source: Removal of tonic inhibition from VTA DA neurons by interneurons and accumbal projections can therefore cause increases in DA neuron activity (Jhou et al., 2009; Johnson and North, 1992) and NAc DA release (van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating disinhibition effects (Jhou et al., 2009; Johnson and North, 1992; van Zessen et al., 2012).

claim: Using a genetically encoded DA reporter confirms that already the very first dose of heroin increases DA in the shell.
source: Using a genetically encoded DA reporter we confirm that already the very first dose of heroin increases DA in the shell.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dLight recordings showing DA increase after first heroin exposure.

claim: In the alternate model of DA-independent reinforcement, the initial effect of opioids would be on VTA GABA neurons that mainly project to the PPN.
source: In the alternate model of DA-independent reinforcement, the initial effect of opioids would still be on VTA GABA neurons that however mainly project to the PPN (Laviolette et al., 2004), a heterogeneous nucleus containing GABA, glutamate and acetylcholine neurons.
evidence: Describes an alternative hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation to Laviolette et al., 2004.

claim: The PPN projects back to the midbrain regulating reinforcement.
source: The PPN projects back to the midbrain (Oakman et al., 1995; Wang and Morales, 2009; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012) regulating reinforcement (Floresco et al., 2003; Inglis et al., 2000; Lammel et al., 2012; Pan and Hyland, 2005; Steidl and Veverka, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies describing PPN-midbrain connectivity and function (Oakman et al., 1995; Wang and Morales, 2009; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Floresco et al., 2003; Inglis et al., 2000; Lammel et al., 2012; Pan and Hyland, 2005; Steidl and Veverka, 2015).

claim: The activation of the LDT-VTA pathway leads to CPP and reinforces operant responses with natural- and drug-rewards.
source: There is direct evidence that the activation of the LDT-VTA pathway leads to CPP, reinforces operant responses with natural- (Lammel et al., 2012; Steidl and Veverka, 2015) and drug-rewards (Shinohara et al., 2014; Wise, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating LDT-VTA pathway function in reinforcement (Lammel et al., 2012; Steidl and Veverka, 2015; Shinohara et al., 2014; Wise, 2004).

claim: All scenarios involving PPN and LDT converge to activate VTA DA neurons, and are thus not DA-independent.
source: However, all these scenarios converge to activate VTA DA neurons, and are thus not DA-independent.
evidence: Inferred from the circuit architecture described, where PPN and LDT pathways ultimately activate VTA DA neurons.

claim: Several publications observe an increase of extracellular DA levels in the shell following acute administration of opioids.
source: Such a 'non-dopaminergic substrate for reward within the VTA' (Nader and van der Kooy, 1997) is also at odds with several publications that observe an increase of extracellular DA levels in the shell following acute administration of opioids (Aragona et al., 2008; Di Chiara and Imperato, 1988; Pontieri et al., 1995; Stuber et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies measuring DA levels after opioid administration (Aragona et al., 2008; Di Chiara and Imperato, 1988; Pontieri et al., 1995; Stuber et al., 2005).

claim: After 12 days of heroin self-administration, inhibition of DA neurons still caused a strong, but fully reversible decrease in the responding behavior.
source: Moreover our data suggest that the same circuits maintain reinforcement as exposure becomes chronic. After 12 days of heroin self-administration, inhibition of DA neurons still caused a strong, but fully reversible decrease in the responding behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic inhibition experiments showing continued requirement for DA neurons after chronic exposure.

claim: DA-independent heroin reinforcement seems unlikely.
source: Taken together DA-independent heroin reinforcement seems unlikely.
evidence: Inferred from the totality of experimental evidence showing DA involvement in heroin reinforcement.

claim: Heroin decreased lever-pressing for VTA DA neuron self-stimulation in a dose-dependent fashion, which could not be explained by sedative effects as the same dose was able to increase locomotor activity in an open field.
source: Heroin decreased lever-pressing for VTA DA neuron self-stimulation (Pascoli et al., 2015) in a dose-dependent fashion, which could not be explained by sedative effects as the same dose was able to increase locomotor activity in an open field.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both optogenetic self-stimulation and open field locomotor testing, with citation to Pascoli et al., 2015.

claim: Occlusion of VTA DA neuron self-stimulation by heroin strongly suggests that heroin converges on the same cellular mechanism.
source: Such occlusion strongly suggests that heroin converges on the same cellular mechanism (similar to cocaine occlusion experiments).
evidence: Inferred from the occlusion experimental design and results, drawing parallel to cocaine experiments.

claim: This study observed strong reinforcement with GABA neuron self-inhibition for the first time in the literature.
source: We also - to the best of our knowledge for the first time in the literature - observed strong reinforcement with GABA neuron self-inhibition, which was sensitive to heroin exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic self-inhibition experiments, claimed as novel finding.

claim: Opioids suppress the activity of VTA GABA interneurons by activation of µ-opioid receptors (MORs).
source: Opioids suppress the activity of VTA GABA interneurons by activation of µ-opioid receptors (MORs) (Jalabert et al., 2011; Johnson and North, 1992; Mazei-Robison et al., 2011), which then hyperpolarize the neurons and decrease the release probability at the axon terminal via the activation of GIRK channels and the inhibition of voltage gated calcium channels, respectively (Cohen et al., 1992; Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies describing MOR-mediated suppression of VTA GABA neurons (Jalabert et al., 2011; Johnson and North, 1992; Mazei-Robison et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 1992).

claim: The IC50 for heroin occlusion of VTA GABA self-inhibition was virtually identical to the IC50 observed with the occlusion of self-stimulation of DA neurons.
source: Interestingly the IC50 for this effect was virtually identical to the IC50 observed with the occlusion of self-stimulation of DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing IC50 values from two different occlusion experiments (6.9 vs 6.4 mg/kg).

claim: The results are in direct contrast with older pharmacological experiments, where DA receptor antagonists had an effect on reinforcement of cocaine but not heroin.
source: Our results are in direct contrast with older pharmacological experiments, where DA receptor antagonists had an effect on reinforcement of cocaine but not heroin (Ettenberg et al., 1982; Pettit et al., 1984).
evidence: Contrasts current findings with previous literature, supported by citations to Ettenberg et al., 1982 and Pettit et al., 1984.

claim: The receptor occupancy of the antagonists in older studies was possibly insufficient, particularly when administered intra-cranially as suggested by the discrepancy between the systemic and intra-cranial results.
source: Maybe the receptor occupancy of the antagonists was insufficient, particularly when administrated intra-cranially as suggested by the discrepancy between the systemic and intra-cranial results (Neisewander et al., 1998).
evidence: Speculative explanation for discrepancy with previous literature, supported by citation to Neisewander et al., 1998.

claim: Electrolytic lesions or inactivation of the NAc result in significantly decreased responding for intravenous self-administration of opioids.
source: Electrolytic lesions or inactivation of the NAc result in significantly decreased responding for intravenous self-administration of opioids (Alderson et al., 2001; Dworkin et al., 1988; Suto et al., 2011; Zito et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing NAc involvement in opioid self-administration (Alderson et al., 2001; Dworkin et al., 1988; Suto et al., 2011; Zito et al., 1985).

claim: Mice learn to self-administer MORs agonists when infused directly into the NAc.
source: Mice also learn to self-administer MORs agonists when infused directly into the NAc (David and Cazala, 2000; Goeders et al., 1984), most likely via the disinhibitory loop connecting the NAc back to the VTA.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing intra-NAc MOR agonist self-administration (David and Cazala, 2000; Goeders et al., 1984), with inference about mechanism.

claim: A recent study using a siRNA to downregulate D1aR in the NAc shell blocked the acquisition of cocaine but not heroin self-administration.
source: A recent study using a siRNA to downregulate D1aR in the NAc shell blocked the acquisition of cocaine but not heroin self-administration (Pisanu et al., 2015), raising the question for the role of specific DA receptors in drug-adaptive behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pisanu et al., 2015 showing differential effects of D1aR downregulation on cocaine vs heroin.

claim: The observation that morphine can induce CPP in DA-deficient mice is likely explained by developmental adaptations.
source: The observation that morphine can induce CPP in DA-deficient mice (Hnasko et al., 2005) is likely explained by developmental adaptations.
evidence: Speculative explanation for findings from Hnasko et al., 2005 showing morphine CPP in DA-deficient mice.

claim: DA-deficient mice suffer from a severe locomotion deficit, which precluded the testing for reinforcement in a self-administration setting.
source: Moreover, these mice suffer from a severe locomotion deficit, which precluded the testing for reinforcement in a self-administration setting.
evidence: Draws from knowledge about DA-deficient mouse phenotype to explain limitations of previous studies.

claim: By confirming the validity of the DA hypotheses for opioids, this study aims to integrate work on these drugs into the emerging circuit model for addiction.
source: Here, by confirming the validity of the DA hypotheses for opioids, we aim to integrate work on these drugs into the emerging circuit model for addiction.
evidence: States the overall goal and interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: This study supports VTA DA neuron disinhibition for opioid reinforcement.
source: Our study thus supports VTA DA neuron disinhibition for the opioid reinforcement.
evidence: Summary conclusion inferred from the totality of experimental evidence presented.

claim: Untangling the circuits underlying opioid reinforcement may allow refining addiction treatments and draft the roadmap for the development of analgesic compounds without addiction liability.
source: Untangling the circuits underlying opioid reinforcement may not only allow refining addiction treatments, but also draft the roadmap for the development of analgesic compounds without addiction liability.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential translational implications of the research findings.

claim: The DA hypothesis of drug reinforcement is rooted in the observation that electrical activation of the medial forebrain bundle leads to repetitive action.
source: The DA hypothesis of drug reinforcement is rooted in the observation that electrical activation of the medial forebrain bundle leads to repetitive action (Olds and Milner, 1954).
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational study by Olds and Milner, 1954.

claim: Rats willingly self-stimulate brain regions populated by DA neurons or receiving inputs from DA neurons.
source: Rats willingly self-stimulate brain regions populated by DA neurons or receiving inputs from DA neurons.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge in the field about self-stimulation behavior.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of DA receptors impairs the reinforcing properties of psychostimulants in both rats and primates.
source: Moreover, pharmacological blockade of DA receptors impairs the reinforcing properties of psychostimulants in both rats (Maldonado et al., 1993; McGregor and Roberts, 1993; Roberts et al., 1977) and primates (Bergman et al., 1989; Johanson and Schuster, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies in rats and primates (Maldonado et al., 1993; McGregor and Roberts, 1993; Roberts et al., 1977; Bergman et al., 1989; Johanson and Schuster, 1975).

claim: Several microdialysis and voltammetry studies demonstrated the increase of DA in the NAc shell as a common feature of addictive drugs, including opioids.
source: Several microdialysis and voltammetry studies demonstrated the increase of DA in the NAc shell as a common feature of addictive drugs, including opioids (Aragona et al., 2008; Di Chiara and Imperato, 1988; Pontieri et al., 1995; Stuber et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies measuring DA levels (Aragona et al., 2008; Di Chiara and Imperato, 1988; Pontieri et al., 1995; Stuber et al., 2005).

claim: Electrolytic lesions of the VTA to NAc pathway decreased reinforcement during intravenous self-administration of morphine and cocaine under a progressive ratio schedule.
source: Furthermore, electrolytic lesions of the VTA to NAc pathway decreased reinforcement during intravenous self-administration of morphine and cocaine under a progressive ratio schedule (Suto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suto et al., 2011 showing effects of VTA-NAc pathway lesions.

claim: The reinforcing effects of opioids require µ-opioid receptors.
source: Indeed, the reinforcing effects of opioids require µ-opioid receptors (Charbogne et al., 2017; Contarino et al., 2002; Matthes et al., 1996), which are enriched in VTA GABA neurons (Cohen et al., 1992; Devine and Wise, 1994; Johnson and North, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing MOR requirement (Charbogne et al., 2017; Contarino et al., 2002; Matthes et al., 1996) and MOR localization (Cohen et al., 1992; Devine and Wise, 1994; Johnson and North, 1992).
